o1.biggest_strength: It opens with what the problem costs (£139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets). It then gives six short one-button messages in our voice, including a post-delivery fit check for bra buyers. The work runs cheapest first, and the savings are shown as ranges with the working.
o1.biggest_mistake: The 2-hour size-switch in the fit-check message depends on an ops capability we may not have. The swap line shows £183,800 of 'sales kept' beside real savings, which could mislead. It is also slightly over the word limit and does not say plainly that fit-finder users may differ from other buyers.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Rank the three fixes by money saved in one line at the top. Say plainly that fit-finder users are self-selected, which is why it uses half the gap. Drop or de-risk the 2-hour switch. Give one realistic net £ figure for the swap change, and trim to 1,000 words.

o2.biggest_strength: It states the decision up front. It puts a fit block in the confirmation for first-time bra buyers. It halves the fit-finder gap for self-selection, includes a hold-out and a conversion guardrail, and gives owners and dates. It also adds a bolder 'ship the swap first' idea with its risk.
o2.biggest_mistake: It has no follow-up fit message after delivery. The day-3 message only goes out if the courier has scanned the parcel, which is thin for the silence problem. It never gives the baseline cost totals or ranks the fixes by money. It also runs over the word limit.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a short post-delivery bra fit nudge. Show the current cost and the saving per fix in order. Make the day-3 message work with or without a scan. Trim to 1,000 words.

reason: Both are accurate and usable, with careful ranges and a holdout. I'd use the first one because its messaging is more complete, with a post-delivery fit check, and it shows what the problem costs me. The second has the sharper test design and the bolder idea, so it was close.
